title: Who originated the Shim Sham Shimmy and George Raft
summary: Green says Willie Bryant had Teddy Blackman teach it to chorus girls as an education dance, and George Raft stole a Dancer's Night while Robinson watched.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: Let me ask you, Chuck, who brought about the Shim-Sham Shimmy? Who originated it?

Well, it was originated by Willie Bryant, partner of Leonard Reed and Ralph Cooper, but he was an orchestra leader so he gave it to the choreographer, Teddy Blackman, to teach to the chorus girls as an education dance. The chorus girls stopped the show doing the Shim-Sham Shimmy, the education dance, and that's what they stopped the show with by all the girls saying, when they come back to take a bow they would say, 'Surprise, that was the education dance.'
What is it about the Shim-Sham Shimmy that makes it more of a feminine-type dance?

Well, it's because, you see, it is really educational in tap dancing because it teaches one how to swing your knees, you see, and what they call the crossing. You see, that was a tap dance they called military tap, see, and that was a very eccentric tap dance, it was very strenuous, you see. But you couldn't let anyone know this -- it was like a soldier going to being grilled, you know, to become a fighting machine, you see. They originated the military tap dance by -- about the Army, you see. It was all hand-me-downs from the Depresssion -- the days of the Depression, see. And it kept going right on through into the prohibition, see. And it was very --
Excuse me, Chuck. Did white dancers learn to do the Shim Sham as well, or was it just mostly, you know, like the Cotton Club.

OH, yes. I'm glad you said white dancers, because there was one white dancer, George Raft -- he come up there and stole the show one night on a Dancer's Night. And Mr. Bill "Bo Jangles" Robinson was sitting in the audience and the spotlight stopped on George Raft -- he looked at Bill "Bo Jangles" Robinson and he said, "I defy him," because Bill "Bo Jangles" Robinson was accepted then as the world's champion tap dancer, and he stopped the show, see.
